name: Judges
v: Jerubbaal — that is, Gideon — was up before dawn with everyone who followed him, and they camped at the spring of Harod. The Midianite camp lay to their north, in the valley below the hill of Moreh.
The LORD said to Gideon, "You have too many fighters with you. If I hand Midian over to this army, Israel will strut back home crowing, 'We saved ourselves.'
So announce to the troops: 'Anyone trembling, anyone afraid — turn around and head home from Mount Gilead.'" Twenty-two thousand walked away. Ten thousand stayed.
The LORD said to Gideon, "Still too many. Take them down to the water. I'll sort them for you there. The one I point to goes with you. The one I reject stays behind."
So Gideon brought them down to the water. The LORD said, "Separate those who lap the water with their tongues like a dog from those who kneel down to drink."
Three hundred lapped from cupped hands. Everyone else dropped to their knees to drink.
The LORD said to Gideon, "With these three hundred who lapped, I will rescue you and deliver Midian into your hand. Send the rest home."
So Gideon took provisions and trumpets from the departing men and sent the Israelites back to their tents — keeping only the three hundred. The Midianite camp lay just below him in the valley.
That night the LORD said to him, "Get up. Go down against the camp. I have given it into your hand.
But if you're afraid to attack, take Purah your servant down with you first.
Listen to what they're saying. After that, you'll find the nerve to strike." So he and Purah crept down to the edge of the armed camp.
Midian, Amalek, and all the desert peoples were sprawled across the valley like locusts — countless, their camels beyond counting, like grains of sand on the seashore.

Gideon arrived just as a man was telling his comrade a dream. "Listen to this," he was saying. "I had a dream — a loaf of barley bread came tumbling into the Midianite camp. It hit the tent, flipped it, knocked it flat, and the whole thing collapsed."
His comrade said, "That can only mean one thing — the sword of Gideon son of Joash, the Israelite. God has handed Midian and the whole camp over to him."
When Gideon heard the dream and its meaning, he dropped to his knees in worship. Then he went back to the Israelite camp and called out, "Up! The LORD has given the Midianite camp into your hand."
He split the three hundred into three companies. Into every man's hand he placed a trumpet and an empty jar with a torch hidden inside.
"Watch me," he said. "Follow my lead. When I reach the edge of the camp, do exactly what I do.
When I blow my trumpet — me and everyone with me — you blow yours, all around the entire camp, and shout, 'For the LORD and for Gideon!'"

Gideon and the hundred men with him reached the edge of the camp just after the middle watch began, right when the new sentries had taken their posts. They blew the trumpets and smashed the jars in their hands.
All three companies blew their trumpets and shattered their jars. They gripped the torches in their left hands, the trumpets in their right, and roared: "A sword for the LORD and for Gideon!"
Each man held his position around the camp. The whole army inside broke — running, screaming, fleeing.

When the three hundred trumpets blasted, the LORD turned every Midianite sword against his own comrade — the whole camp tearing itself apart. The army ran toward Beth-shittah, toward Zererah, all the way to the edge of Abel-meholah near Tabbath.
The men of Israel were summoned — from Naphtali, from Asher, from all Manasseh — and they chased Midian down.

Gideon sent runners throughout the hill country of Ephraim with the message: "Come down against Midian. Seize the waters ahead of them, all the way to Beth-barah, and the Jordan." So every man of Ephraim mustered and seized the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.

They captured two Midianite commanders, Oreb and Zeeb. They killed Oreb at the rock that now bears his name, and Zeeb at the winepress that bears his. They hunted Midian down, and brought the heads of Oreb and Zeeb to Gideon on the other side of the Jordan.

com.d:
# Judges 7: The Victory of Faith Over Fear

Gideon's final test reveals a spiritual principle that runs counter to human instinct: God's strength is made perfect in our weakness, and faith flourishes when earthly resources fail. This passage teaches us that the Lord doesn't need our numbers—he needs our trust.

By the time Gideon gathers his army of thirty-two thousand men, fear has already done its quiet work. God's instruction to release the afraid cuts the force to ten thousand. Then, through an unusual test at the water, the number shrinks to three hundred. What began as overwhelming inadequacy becomes something worse—apparent absurdity. Yet here lies the genius of God's design. With such a small band, Gideon cannot credit human strength for victory. No one will boast that their sword saved Israel. The glory belongs entirely to the Lord.

This pattern repeats throughout Scripture because human hearts struggle with the same temptation: to trust what we can see and count and control. We want enough resources, enough talent, enough time, enough people. We want the math to work out in our favor before we step forward. But faith means moving when the numbers don't add up, when circumstances whisper that failure is certain.

Notice that God doesn't ask Gideon to be reckless. The three hundred are equipped and positioned with care. The trumpets, jars, and torches are deliberate—strange weapons, yes, but purposeful. Faith isn't foolishness; it's clear-eyed obedience partnered with trust in God's character.

How many times do we disqualify ourselves from God's work because we lack what seems necessary? Perhaps you're convinced you're too weak, too small, too inexperienced for what God is calling you toward. The story of Gideon's three hundred whispers a different truth: your insufficiency is precisely where God's sufficiency becomes visible.

What is God calling you to do that seems impossible by ordinary measures—and how might your weakness become the occasion for displaying his strength?
com.s:
The seventh chapter of Judges presents the celebrated account of Gideon's victory over the Midianites, a narrative that stands as one of the most theologically significant episodes in the Deuteronomistic History. Composed during the monarchic period but reflecting earlier oral traditions, this chapter demonstrates the characteristic theological motif of divine deliverance through human weakness, a theme that pervades the entire book of Judges.

The narrative opens with the dramatic reduction of Gideon's army from 32,000 to a mere 300 warriors, a process occurring at the spring of Harod near the hill of Moreh. The divine rationale is explicitly stated: "lest Israel vaunt themselves against me, saying, mine own hand hath saved me" (v. 2). The Hebrew verb *yitpā'ēr* (to glorify oneself) emphasizes the theological concern with proper attribution of military victory. This systematic reduction serves the Deuteronomistic purpose of demonstrating that Israel's security depends not on military strength but on faithful dependence upon Yahweh.

The selection criterion involving water consumption (vv. 5–7) has generated considerable scholarly debate. The distinction between those who lap water "as a dog lappeth" versus those who kneel has been variously interpreted as testing alertness, military readiness, or perhaps representing an arbitrary selection emphasizing divine sovereignty. The Hebrew *mĕlaqĕqîm* (those who lap) may suggest either vigilance or, conversely, represent those less naturally suited for warfare, further underscoring the miraculous nature of the subsequent victory.

The nocturnal assault employing trumpets (*šôpārôt*), empty pitchers, and torches represents unconventional warfare designed to create confusion among the Midianite camp. The battle cry "The sword of the LORD and of Gideon" (v. 20) encapsulates the partnership between divine initiative and human agency characteristic of holy war traditions. The resulting panic causes the Midianites to turn against one another, a motif appearing elsewhere in biblical conquest narratives.

Within the broader Judges framework, this chapter illustrates the cyclical pattern of apostasy, oppression, crying out, and deliverance. The passage anticipates later prophetic critiques of military self-reliance and resonates with the New Testament affirmation that divine power operates through human weakness.
com.p:
Judges 7 unfolds approximately 1150 years before Christ's birth, during the turbulent era of Israel's judges—a period spanning roughly three centuries after Joshua's conquest and before the establishment of the monarchy under Saul. This chapter records Gideon's dramatic victory over the Midianite oppressors, situated within the larger pattern of Israel's cyclical unfaithfulness during the dark days when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes." Within the grand redemptive arc, this moment stands between the Exodus deliverance and the coming Kingdom, serving as a vivid foreshadowing of how God would ultimately accomplish salvation—not through human might but through divine power made perfect in weakness.

The systematic reduction of Gideon's army from 32,000 to a mere 300 warriors constitutes one of Scripture's most striking displays of divine sovereignty in redemption. The Lord explicitly states His purpose: "lest Israel boast over me, saying, 'My own hand has saved me.'" Here the prophetic pattern emerges with unmistakable clarity. Just as Yahweh deliberately stripped away numerical advantage so that victory would be attributed to Him alone, so too the cross would appear as utter weakness and foolishness to watching principalities. The 300 with their torches, clay jars, and trumpets prefigure the apostolic band carrying gospel light in earthen vessels, their proclamation shattering darkness and routing spiritual forces far mightier than themselves.

The clay jars broken to reveal hidden light bear profound typological weight. Paul explicitly invokes this imagery when he writes of treasure in jars of clay, the life of Jesus manifested through mortal flesh. Gideon's warriors conquered not by wielding swords but by breaking vessels—their very vulnerability becoming the instrument of revelation. So Christ Himself was broken, His body given, that the light of God's glory might blaze forth in redemptive splendor. The Midianites turned their swords against one another in confusion, just as the cross turned Satan's weapon of death into the instrument of his own destruction.

The trumpet blast and the cry "The sword of the LORD and of Gideon" echo forward to the final trumpet when Christ returns as conquering King. What was accomplished typologically in Canaan, fulfilled decisively at Calvary, awaits consummation when every enemy is placed beneath His feet.

For the church dwelling between the advents, this chapter declares that God's kingdom advances not through worldly power but through Spirit-empowered weakness, broken vessels radiating resurrection light until the dawn of everlasting victory.
